frameworks.name: Outbound vs. Inbound Sales Team Separation
frameworks.definition: Structurally separate door-knocking (outbound) and lead-fed (inbound) sales teams to prevent lazy skill atrophy and enable high-velocity close-rate optimization.

frameworks.name: Sales Career Progression as Graduation Path
frameworks.definition: High-performing outbound salespeople graduate to inbound lead-fed work as a promotion tier, with higher-volume, lower-commission rates offset by reliability and reduced stress.

claims.text: When outbound (door-knocking) and inbound (lead-fed) sales teams are mixed, inbound salespeople default to easier lead work, causing door-knocking prospecting to collapse because buying leads appears more convenient than street work (More Mozi's roofing business, summer 2024).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Effort preference: inbound work (leads pre-qualified, calendar-stacked) requires less street time, incentivizing abandonment of higher-friction outbound work when both are available.
bounded_by: Does not apply when inbound and outbound are structurally separated with different comp structures

claims.text: Purchased lead acquisition cost (CAC) of $7,500 per customer does not work when average customer lifetime value is $6,500 (More Mozi's roofing business, summer 2024).
claims.speaker: More Mozi
bounded_by: Specific to unqualified purchased leads; does not apply to door-knocking or insurance-driven storm lead generation

claims.text: In high-touch service sales (e.g., residential roofing), only salespeople who consistently close cold prospects ("savages") should ever graduate to lead-fed inbound work; feeding expensive qualified leads to inconsistent closers wastes the most expensive inventory (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: close rate is the primary variable
claims.mechanism: Qualified leads are the highest-value sales asset; feeding them to sub-100% closer wastes margin. Only proven closers preserve lead value.
bounded_by: Does not apply to high-volume e-commerce or self-serve SaaS where conversion math is forgiving

claims.text: Inbound (lead-fed) sales roles should carry different commission structures than outbound door-knocking: lower per-deal percentage but higher total volume and reliability, because inbound reps close 5+ deals per day versus 0-3 in outbound, reducing earnings variance (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: outbound team still exists for comparison
claims.mechanism: Inbound allows vertical stacking of pre-qualified leads; outbound requires door-to-door prospecting with zero guaranteed daily meetings. Reliability attracts family-focused salespeople who value income predictability over upside.
bounded_by: Assumes pre-qualified lead quality; poor-quality leads compress inbound volume

claims.text: When scaling a new sales channel (e.g., purchased-lead roofing), start with one proven high-closer, not multiple new hires, to minimize iteration variables and isolate whether the bottleneck is the offer / lead source or the sales process (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each new hire adds process risk; if you have one known closer, failures are traceable to offer/lead-source, not rep inconsistency. This accelerates iteration.
bounded_by: Does not apply at scale (past $5M revenue) where process standardization is mandatory

claims.text: A roofing contractor's core business (door-to-door lead generation, inbound sales, sales process) is the two-to-three revenue-critical elements that must remain in-house; hiring a competent marketing director costs more than expected but is non-negotiable for scaling past the founder bottleneck (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Founder cannot simultaneously optimize marketing AND train sales team; splitting these into role ownership allows both levers to compound. Underpaying for marketing perpetuates founder-dependent lead generation.
bounded_by: Does not imply outsourcing; in-house hires are required for strategy velocity

claims.text: The trade-off between hiring a $100k annual replacement person and spending $6,000 per month on contractor marketing services favors the $100k hire, because core business functions (sales, marketing) determine ceiling (Alex Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business is constrained by marketing quality, not cost
claims.mechanism: A competent full-time marketer compounds improvements iteratively; contractors optimize per-engagement but lack continuity and skin-in-game. Full-time hire ownership > part-time service.
bounded_by: Assumes hire is genuinely competent; a bad $100k hire is worse than any contractor

claims.text: Purchased-lead roofing sales campaigns fail not because roofing CAC is inherently bad, but because unqualified purchased leads ($7,500 CAC) are being fed to salespeople accustomed to door-knocking cold prospects (high-threshold closers), creating offer/lead-source iteration impossible (More Mozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Door-knockers expect resistance and are trained to overcome objections. Pre-qualified inbound leads have different objection patterns (price, timeline) that outbound-trained reps mishandle. Wrong sales motion = wasted leads, not wrong lead source.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the sales motion is optimized for each channel separately

claims.text: When a business transitions from insurance-funded storm lead generation to retail roofing (non-insurance), door-knocking weight increases on the team because retail prospects require higher-touch qualification and have fewer motivated-buyer signals than storm/insurance-driven leads (More Mozi).
claims.speaker: More Mozi
conditions: storm lead generation model is disrupted (climate change, fewer storms)
claims.mechanism: Insurance-covered storm damage creates immediate pain (urgent need, pre-approved insurance funding). Retail roofing requires reps to manufacture demand (cold prospect, price-sensitive, no external funding). Same door-knocking motion, higher effort per contact.
bounded_by: Specific to property services; does not apply to pre-motivated insurance leads

claims.text: A door-knocking business should be non-binary about lead sources: do NOT reject purchased leads as sacrilege (religious belief against inbound); instead, test them in isolation with controlled variables to validate whether lead quality or sales motion is the bottleneck (Alex Hormozi, addressing More Mozi's limiting beliefs).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has strong belief against inbound/purchased leads
primary channel (door-knocking) is failing due to external factors
claims.mechanism: Cognitive rigidity ('leads from doors only') prevents testing. Testing purchased leads with one strong closer allows iteration without committing the whole team.
bounded_by: Testing must be isolated; mixing teams ruins variable isolation

claims.text: Marketing agencies using AI tools and high-level automation without in-house optimization knowledge produce mediocre lead sources ($7,500+ CAC) because they lack owner-level accountability for channel unit economics (More Mozi's experience with external agencies).
claims.speaker: More Mozi
conditions: younger marketing agencies using automated tools
claims.mechanism: Agencies optimize for lead volume and ad spend velocity, not profitability per customer. Without direct ROI accountability (they profit from ad spend, not customer LTV), incentives are misaligned.
bounded_by: Does not imply AI tools are inherently bad; rather, misaligned incentives between agency growth and business profitability

examples.text: More Mozi's roofing company had built a 100% door-to-door lead-generation machine, hitting $5M revenue for two years, until storm patterns disappeared in the Metro Detroit market due to climate change. The company pivoted to retail residential roofing, but the sales team that thrived on weather-driven insurance leads struggled with cold retail prospects. In October 2024, More Mozi bought purchased leads to fill the pipeline gap, spending $7,500 per customer acquisition. Initial results showed culture shift (reps were happier with stacked calendars) but unit economics were catastrophic: $7,500 CAC against $6,500 LTV. The failure was misattributed to 'purchased leads are bad' rather than diagnosed as a team separation and sales-motion problem.

A roofing contractor uses external marketing agencies staffed with younger practitioners deploying AI tools and high-level CRM software to generate leads. The contractor measured $7,500 per customer acquisition cost with $6,500 average customer value, a clear failure. The agencies were optimizing for ad volume and spend velocity, not customer profitability, because their incentives are commission-on-spend, not owner-level ROI accountability.

When a proven door-knocking salesperson is promoted to inbound (lead-fed) work, they experience a dramatic workload shift: instead of 1-3 closes per day from street work, they can close 5-7 customers per day from pre-qualified calendar slots. Even if per-deal commission drops (e.g., from 10% to 6%), total income remains flat or rises because volume scales 3-5x, while stress and weather-exposure drop. This transition is attractive to reps with families who value income predictability.

practices.text: Separate outbound (door-knocking) and inbound (lead-fed) sales teams structurally; do not feed qualified leads to reps who have not proven they can close cold prospects.
When testing a new sales channel or lead source, start with one proven closer and iterate on offer/lead quality; adding multiple new hires multiplies iteration variables and obscures the bottleneck.
Hire a competent full-time marketing director rather than using agency contractors for core go-to-market strategy; full-time ownership compounds better than per-engagement contractor services.
Test purchased leads in isolation with controlled variables; reject neither door-knocking nor inbound leads categorically based on founder belief.
Design inbound sales comp structures differently from outbound (lower per-deal %, higher volume stability) to account for the reliability and risk profile of pre-qualified lead work.
